FA3

Espiritu, Joseph Raphael, M.

2026-08-28

Part A. Define Your Multivariate Normal Distribution — 6 points

We define our simulated population as

\[ X\sim N_3(\mu,\Sigma). \]

This notation describes the joint distribution of our three variables.

Here, \(X\) is a random vector containing the three delivery-operation variables:

\[ X= \begin{bmatrix} X_1\\ X_2\\ X_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \text{Distance}\\ \text{Delivery Time}\\ \text{Fuel Used} \end{bmatrix}. \]

The three components are defined as

\[ X_1=\text{delivery distance (km)}, \]

\[ X_2=\text{delivery time (minutes)}, \]

\[ X_3=\text{fuel consumed (liters)}. \]

The subscript \(3\) in \(N_3\) indicates that the distribution has three variables or dimensions.

The vector \(\mu\) represents the mean vector, which determines the center of the distribution:

\[ \mu= \begin{bmatrix} \mu_1\\ \mu_2\\ \mu_3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The matrix \(\Sigma\) represents the covariance matrix. Its diagonal elements describe the individual variances of the three variables, while its off-diagonal elements describe how pairs of variables vary together.

Therefore,

\[ X\sim N_3(\mu,\Sigma) \]

means that we are modeling the three delivery variables jointly, with their center determined by \(\mu\) and their variability and relationships determined by \(\Sigma\).

For this simulation, we use a delivery operations scenario because distance, delivery time, and fuel consumption have a reasonable operational relationship. A longer delivery distance can generally require more time and fuel, so we expect positive relationships among these variables.

A.1 The Variables and Their Interpretation

Our random vector is

\[ X= \begin{bmatrix} X_1\\ X_2\\ X_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \text{Distance}\\ \text{Delivery Time}\\ \text{Fuel Used} \end{bmatrix}. \]

The three variables are summarized below.

Variable Symbol Unit Interpretation
Delivery distance \(X_1\) km Distance traveled for a delivery
Delivery time \(X_2\) minutes Time required to complete the delivery
Fuel consumed \(X_3\) liters Fuel used during the delivery

The purpose of defining these variables together is to investigate not only their individual distributions but also how they vary jointly through covariance and correlation.

A.2 The Mean Vector \(\mu\)

We choose the following theoretical mean vector:

\[ \mu= \begin{bmatrix} 12\\ 35\\ 4.5 \end{bmatrix}. \]

This means that the theoretical population has:

  • an average delivery distance of \(12\) km;
  • an average delivery time of \(35\) minutes;
  • an average fuel consumption of \(4.5\) L.

Thus, the center of our simulated population is

\[ \boxed{\mu=(12,35,4.5)' }. \]

We define the mean vector in R as follows:

mu <- c(
  Distance_km = 12,
  Delivery_Time_min = 35,
  Fuel_Liters = 4.5
)

mu
##       Distance_km Delivery_Time_min       Fuel_Liters 
##              12.0              35.0               4.5

A.3 The Covariance Matrix \(\Sigma\)

We choose the covariance matrix

\[ \Sigma= \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 12 & 2.7\\ 12 & 64 & 7.2\\ 2.7 & 7.2 & 2.25 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The diagonal elements represent the variances of the three variables:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(X_1)=9, \]

\[ \operatorname{Var}(X_2)=64, \]

\[ \operatorname{Var}(X_3)=2.25. \]

Therefore, their theoretical standard deviations are

\[ \sigma_1=\sqrt{9}=3, \]

\[ \sigma_2=\sqrt{64}=8, \]

\[ \sigma_3=\sqrt{2.25}=1.5. \]

The off-diagonal elements represent the covariances between the variables:

\[ \operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)=12, \]

\[ \operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_3)=2.7, \]

\[ \operatorname{Cov}(X_2,X_3)=7.2. \]

All three covariances are positive, indicating that larger values of one variable tend to be associated with larger values of the other variable. For example, longer delivery distances tend to be associated with longer delivery times and greater fuel consumption.

We define the covariance matrix in R:

Sigma <- matrix(
  c(
    9, 12, 2.7,
    12, 64, 7.2,
    2.7, 7.2, 2.25
  ),
  nrow = 3,
  byrow = TRUE
)

rownames(Sigma) <- names(mu)
colnames(Sigma) <- names(mu)

Sigma
##                   Distance_km Delivery_Time_min Fuel_Liters
## Distance_km               9.0              12.0        2.70
## Delivery_Time_min        12.0              64.0        7.20
## Fuel_Liters               2.7               7.2        2.25

Our simulated population is therefore

\[ \boxed{ X\sim N_3 \left( \begin{bmatrix} 12\\ 35\\ 4.5 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 12 & 2.7\\ 12 & 64 & 7.2\\ 2.7 & 7.2 & 2.25 \end{bmatrix} \right) }. \]

A.4 The Corresponding Correlation Matrix

Covariance depends on the measurement scales of the variables. To describe the strength of the linear relationships in a standardized form, we calculate the correlation matrix.

The correlation between two variables is

\[ \rho_{ij} = \frac{\sigma_{ij}} {\sqrt{\sigma_{ii}\sigma_{jj}}}. \]

For delivery distance and delivery time,

\[ \rho_{12} = \frac{12}{\sqrt{9(64)}} = \frac{12}{24} = 0.50. \]

For delivery distance and fuel consumption,

\[ \rho_{13} = \frac{2.7}{\sqrt{9(2.25)}} = 0.60. \]

For delivery time and fuel consumption,

\[ \rho_{23} = \frac{7.2}{\sqrt{64(2.25)}} = 0.60. \]

Therefore, the theoretical correlation matrix is

\[ R= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0.50 & 0.60\\ 0.50 & 1 & 0.60\\ 0.60 & 0.60 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

We calculate it in R using cov2cor():

R_theoretical <- cov2cor(Sigma)

round(R_theoretical, 3)
##                   Distance_km Delivery_Time_min Fuel_Liters
## Distance_km               1.0               0.5         0.6
## Delivery_Time_min         0.5               1.0         0.6
## Fuel_Liters               0.6               0.6         1.0

The positive correlations mean that we expect an upward relationship between the variables in the simulated data. In particular, the correlations of \(0.60\) indicate somewhat stronger positive relationships than the correlation of \(0.50\). Unlike covariance, correlation is standardized and therefore provides a more directly comparable measure of linear relationship between variables with different units.

A.5 Why Is Our Covariance Matrix Appropriate?

The covariance matrix is appropriate for our simulation for several reasons.

First, it is symmetric, since

\[ \Sigma=\Sigma'. \]

This is necessary for a covariance matrix.

is_symmetric <- isTRUE(all.equal(Sigma, t(Sigma)))

is_symmetric
## [1] TRUE

Second, the covariance matrix must be positive definite for our multivariate normal model. We can check this using its eigenvalues.

eigenvalues <- eigen(Sigma, symmetric = TRUE)$values

round(eigenvalues, 6)
## [1] 67.391100  6.747335  1.111565

All of the eigenvalues are positive, so \(\Sigma\) is positive definite.

We can also check that its determinant is positive:

det(Sigma)
## [1] 505.44

The determinant is also positive, which is consistent with the matrix being valid. More importantly, the positive eigenvalues confirm that \(\Sigma\) is positive definite.

From a scenario perspective, the matrix is also appropriate because its positive covariance values represent the expected operational relationships among distance, delivery time, and fuel consumption.

Therefore, the covariance matrix is mathematically valid because it is symmetric and positive definite, and it is also reasonable for our logistics scenario because its positive covariance values represent plausible relationships among distance, delivery time, and fuel consumption.

Part B. Generate and Explore the Simulated Data — 8 points

In Part A, we defined our theoretical population as

\[ X\sim N_3(\mu,\Sigma), \]

with

\[ \mu= \begin{bmatrix} 12\\ 35\\ 4.5 \end{bmatrix} \]

and

\[ \Sigma= \begin{bmatrix} 9&12&2.7\\ 12&64&7.2\\ 2.7&7.2&2.25 \end{bmatrix}. \]

In Part B, we now generate a random sample from this population.

The purpose of this simulation is to determine whether the sample statistics and graphical patterns are reasonably consistent with the theoretical parameters that we specified in Part A.

B.1 Generate the Simulated Data

The FA3 instructions require at least

\[ n=1000 \]

observations. We use

\[ \boxed{n=5000} \]

for our simulation.

We use 5,000 observations so that we have a sufficiently large sample for comparing the simulated statistics with the theoretical population parameters.

Each observation contains three values:

\[ (X_1,X_2,X_3), \]

representing delivery distance, delivery time, and fuel consumption.

We generate the observations using the same \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\) that we defined in Part A.

n <- 5000

X <- MASS::mvrnorm(
  n = n,
  mu = mu,
  Sigma = Sigma
)

X <- as.data.frame(X)

colnames(X) <- names(mu)

head(X)
##   Distance_km Delivery_Time_min Fuel_Liters
## 1    17.08124          32.49193    5.715249
## 2    15.21081          42.70414    7.113503
## 3    14.47867          47.72501    3.875052
## 4    12.13101          48.51689    5.641261
## 5    11.85813          46.29903    6.562272
## 6    14.49613          41.29887    5.167525

The resulting dataset contains 5,000 simulated delivery observations and three variables.

We can also check the dimensions of the simulated dataset:

dim(X)
## [1] 5000    3

The expected result is

\[ 5000\times3, \]

because there are 5,000 observations and three variables.

B.2 Simulated Means

In Part A, we specified the theoretical mean vector as

\[ \mu= \begin{bmatrix} 12\\ 35\\ 4.5 \end{bmatrix}. \]

We now calculate the corresponding means from the simulated sample.

The sample mean vector is

\[ \bar X= \begin{bmatrix} \bar X_1\\ \bar X_2\\ \bar X_3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

sample_means <- colMeans(X)

round(sample_means, 3)
##       Distance_km Delivery_Time_min       Fuel_Liters 
##            11.995            35.060             4.496

What do we expect?

Because the observations were generated from the population with mean vector \(\mu\), we expect

\[ \bar X\approx\mu. \]

Therefore, we expect the simulated means to be reasonably close to

\[ 12,\quad35,\quad4.5. \]

B.3 Simulated Variances

The diagonal elements of our theoretical covariance matrix from Part A are

\[ \sigma_{11}=9, \]

\[ \sigma_{22}=64, \]

and

\[ \sigma_{33}=2.25. \]

Therefore, the theoretical variances are

\[ 9,\quad64,\quad2.25. \]

We calculate the sample variances from the simulated observations.

sample_variances <- sapply(X, var)

round(sample_variances, 3)
##       Distance_km Delivery_Time_min       Fuel_Liters 
##             9.081            63.561             2.248

We expect

\[ S_{11}\approx9, \]

\[ S_{22}\approx64, \]

and

\[ S_{33}\approx2.25. \]

Again, the simulated values will not necessarily be exactly equal to the theoretical values because of random sampling.

B.4 Simulated Covariance Matrix

We now calculate the covariance matrix of the simulated observations.

sample_covariances <- cov(X)

round(sample_covariances, 3)
##                   Distance_km Delivery_Time_min Fuel_Liters
## Distance_km             9.081            12.157       2.699
## Delivery_Time_min      12.157            63.561       7.251
## Fuel_Liters             2.699             7.251       2.248

Recall that the theoretical covariance matrix from Part A is

\[ \Sigma= \begin{bmatrix} 9&12&2.7\\ 12&64&7.2\\ 2.7&7.2&2.25 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, we expect the simulated covariance matrix to be reasonably close to \(\Sigma\).

In particular, we expect the off-diagonal elements to remain positive:

\[ S_{12}\approx12, \]

\[ S_{13}\approx2.7, \]

\[ S_{23}\approx7.2. \]

This would indicate that the simulated variables retain the positive relationships specified in Part A.

B.5 Simulated Correlation Matrix

In Part A, we calculated the theoretical correlation matrix

\[ R= \begin{bmatrix} 1&0.50&0.60\\ 0.50&1&0.60\\ 0.60&0.60&1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

We now calculate the correlation matrix from the simulated observations.

sample_correlations <- cor(X)

round(sample_correlations, 3)
##                   Distance_km Delivery_Time_min Fuel_Liters
## Distance_km             1.000             0.506       0.597
## Delivery_Time_min       0.506             1.000       0.607
## Fuel_Liters             0.597             0.607       1.000

We expect the simulated correlations to be close to the theoretical values:

\[ \rho_{12}=0.50, \]

\[ \rho_{13}=0.60, \]

\[ \rho_{23}=0.60. \]

The diagonal entries are 1 because each variable has a correlation of 1 with itself.

The important values for examining dependence between different variables are the off-diagonal entries.

B.6 Theoretical versus Simulated Results

We now combine the theoretical and simulated means and variances into one table.

comparison <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(mu),
  Theoretical_Mean = as.numeric(mu),
  Simulated_Mean = as.numeric(sample_means),
  Theoretical_Variance = diag(Sigma),
  Simulated_Variance = as.numeric(sample_variances)
)

comparison$Mean_Difference <-
  comparison$Simulated_Mean -
  comparison$Theoretical_Mean

comparison$Variance_Difference <-
  comparison$Simulated_Variance -
  comparison$Theoretical_Variance

knitr::kable(
  comparison,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Theoretical versus simulated means and variances"
)
Theoretical versus simulated means and variances
Variable Theoretical_Mean Simulated_Mean Theoretical_Variance Simulated_Variance Mean_Difference Variance_Difference
Distance_km Distance_km 12.0 11.995 9.00 9.081 -0.005 0.081
Delivery_Time_min Delivery_Time_min 35.0 35.060 64.00 63.561 0.060 -0.439
Fuel_Liters Fuel_Liters 4.5 4.496 2.25 2.248 -0.004 -0.002

We can also compare the theoretical and simulated correlation matrices directly.

correlation_comparison <- data.frame(
  Variable_Pair = c(
    "Distance - Delivery Time",
    "Distance - Fuel",
    "Delivery Time - Fuel"
  ),
  Theoretical_Correlation = c(
    R_theoretical[1, 2],
    R_theoretical[1, 3],
    R_theoretical[2, 3]
  ),
  Simulated_Correlation = c(
    sample_correlations[1, 2],
    sample_correlations[1, 3],
    sample_correlations[2, 3]
  )
)

correlation_comparison$Difference <-
  correlation_comparison$Simulated_Correlation -
  correlation_comparison$Theoretical_Correlation

knitr::kable(
  correlation_comparison,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Theoretical versus simulated correlations"
)
Theoretical versus simulated correlations
Variable_Pair Theoretical_Correlation Simulated_Correlation Difference
Distance - Delivery Time 0.5 0.506 0.006
Distance - Fuel 0.6 0.597 -0.003
Delivery Time - Fuel 0.6 0.607 0.007

Why are we comparing these values?

Part A gave us the theoretical population parameters.

Part B gives us a random sample from that population.

Therefore, we are checking whether

\[ \bar X\approx\mu \]

and

\[ S\approx\Sigma. \]

Overall, the simulated means, variances, covariances, and correlations are reasonably close to their theoretical counterparts. The small differences are expected from random sampling and do not indicate a problem with the simulation.

B.7 Visualization: Scatterplot Matrix

pairs(
  X,
  main = "Part B: Scatterplot Matrix of Simulated Delivery Variables",
  pch = 16,
  cex = 0.45
)

What are we looking for?

The scatterplot matrix allows us to examine the relationships between each pair of variables.

From Part A, we specified positive correlations:

\[ \rho_{12}=0.50, \qquad \rho_{13}=0.60, \qquad \rho_{23}=0.60. \]

Therefore, we expect the pairwise point clouds to generally have an upward orientation.

The relationships with correlation \(0.60\) should show a somewhat stronger linear pattern than the relationship with correlation \(0.50\).

The scatterplot matrix shows upward-oriented point clouds for all three variable pairs, which is consistent with the positive correlations specified in Part A. The relationships involving fuel consumption appear somewhat stronger than the distance–delivery-time relationship, consistent with the theoretical correlations of 0.60 compared with 0.50.

B.8 Visualization: Histograms

We now examine the three variables individually using histograms.

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

hist(
  X$Distance_km,
  breaks = 30,
  main = "Delivery Distance",
  xlab = "Distance (km)"
)

hist(
  X$Delivery_Time_min,
  breaks = 30,
  main = "Delivery Time",
  xlab = "Time (minutes)"
)

hist(
  X$Fuel_Liters,
  breaks = 30,
  main = "Fuel Consumption",
  xlab = "Fuel (liters)"
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

These histograms allow us to examine the individual variables.

\[ 12,\quad35,\quad4.5. \]

The three histograms are approximately bell-shaped and centered near their theoretical means of 12 km, 35 minutes, and 4.5 L. Their spreads are also consistent with the theoretical standard deviations of 3, 8, and 1.5. This provides visual evidence that the individual simulated variables follow the intended normal distributions.

The histograms provide a univariate view, while the scatterplot matrix from the previous section allows us to examine the variables jointly.

B.9 Visualization: Correlation Matrix

We can also visualize the simulated correlation matrix.

First, install the corrplot package if it has not already been installed:

install.packages("corrplot")

Then load the package:

library(corrplot)

We can now create a correlation plot:

corrplot(
  sample_correlations,
  method = "color",
  addCoef.col = "black",
  tl.col = "black",
  number.cex = 0.9,
  title = "Part B: Simulated Correlation Matrix",
  mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0)
)

The correlation plot is a visual representation of the same correlation matrix calculated earlier using

cor(X)

The diagonal entries are 1 because each variable is perfectly correlated with itself.

The off-diagonal entries are the relationships that we are most interested in:

\[ \rho_{12}, \qquad \rho_{13}, \qquad \rho_{23}. \]

The simulated correlation plot shows positive off-diagonal correlations for all three variable pairs, with values of approximately 050, 0.60, and 0.59. This visually confirms the positive dependence observed numerically in the correlation matrix.

B.10 Part B Interpretation

The simulation generated 5,000 observations from the multivariate normal population defined in Part A.

The theoretical mean vector was

\[ \mu= \begin{bmatrix} 12\\ 35\\ 4.5 \end{bmatrix}, \]

and the theoretical covariance matrix was

\[ \Sigma= \begin{bmatrix} 9&12&2.7\\ 12&64&7.2\\ 2.7&7.2&2.25 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The simulated means can be compared with the theoretical means, while the simulated variances and covariances can be compared with the corresponding elements of \(\Sigma\).

The simulated correlations can also be compared with the theoretical values

\[ 0.50,\quad0.60,\quad0.60. \]

Overall, the simulation successfully reproduces the theoretical population defined in Part A. The simulated means are very close to 12, 35, and 4.5, while the simulated variances, covariances, and correlations are also reasonably close to their theoretical values. The scatterplot matrix shows the expected positive relationships, and the histograms show approximately normal individual distributions centered near their theoretical means. These results indicate that the 5,000 simulated observations behave consistently with the specified multivariate normal model.

Part C. Investigate the Effect of Correlation — 7 points

In Part A, we defined the covariance and correlation structure of our delivery-operation variables. In Part B, we generated observations from that distribution and examined the resulting relationships.

In this part, we want to investigate more directly:

How does changing the correlation affect the shape and orientation of the simulated observations?

\[ \boxed{\rho=0.25,\qquad \rho=0.50,\qquad \rho=0.75}. \]

These values allow us to observe a gradual increase in positive correlation:

  • \(\rho=0.25\): weak positive correlation;
  • \(\rho=0.50\): moderate positive correlation;
  • \(\rho=0.75\): strong positive correlation.

The purpose is to see how these different correlation structures affect the simulated observations.

C.1 Keep the Other Parameters Controlled

To investigate the effect of correlation, we keep the other parameters from Part A fixed.

Our mean vector remains

\[ \mu= \begin{bmatrix} 12\\ 35\\ 4.5 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The standard deviations also remain fixed:

\[ \sigma_1=3,\qquad \sigma_2=8,\qquad \sigma_3=1.5. \]

Therefore, the main parameter that changes between our three simulations is the correlation.

This allows us to make a more direct comparison between the three simulated distributions.

correlation_levels <- c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75)

standard_deviations <- sqrt(diag(Sigma))

standard_deviations
##       Distance_km Delivery_Time_min       Fuel_Liters 
##               3.0               8.0               1.5

C.2 Construct the Correlation Matrices

For each selected value of \(\rho\), we construct a correlation matrix of the form

\[ R_\rho= \begin{bmatrix} 1&\rho&\rho\\ \rho&1&\rho\\ \rho&\rho&1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The diagonal entries remain 1 because each variable is perfectly correlated with itself.

The off-diagonal entries are the correlations between different variables, and these are what we change.

For \(\rho=0.25\),

\[ R_{0.25}= \begin{bmatrix} 1&0.25&0.25\\ 0.25&1&0.25\\ 0.25&0.25&1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

For \(\rho=0.50\),

\[ R_{0.50}= \begin{bmatrix} 1&0.50&0.50\\ 0.50&1&0.50\\ 0.50&0.50&1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

For \(\rho=0.75\),

\[ R_{0.75}= \begin{bmatrix} 1&0.75&0.75\\ 0.75&1&0.75\\ 0.75&0.75&1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Thus, as \(\rho\) increases, the positive relationship between the variables becomes stronger.

C.3 Convert the Correlation Matrix to a Covariance Matrix

The simulation function requires a covariance matrix. We therefore convert each correlation matrix into a covariance matrix while keeping our standard deviations fixed.

The relationship between the covariance matrix and correlation matrix is

\[ \Sigma=DRD, \]

where \(D\) is the diagonal matrix containing the standard deviations.

For our variables,

\[ D= \begin{bmatrix} 3&0&0\\ 0&8&0\\ 0&0&1.5 \end{bmatrix}. \]

We create a function that performs this conversion for each selected correlation value.

D <- diag(standard_deviations)

create_covariance_matrix <- function(rho) {

  R_rho <- matrix(
    rho,
    nrow = 3,
    ncol = 3
  )

  diag(R_rho) <- 1

  Sigma_rho <- D %*% R_rho %*% D

  return(Sigma_rho)
}

For example, the covariance matrix corresponding to \(\rho=0.50\) is:

Sigma_050 <- create_covariance_matrix(0.50)

round(Sigma_050, 3)
##       [,1] [,2] [,3]
## [1,]  9.00   12 2.25
## [2,] 12.00   64 6.00
## [3,]  2.25    6 2.25

The diagonal remains

\[ 9,\quad64,\quad2.25, \]

because the variances are being kept fixed.

Only the covariance values change as the correlation changes.

For example, when \(\rho=0.50\),

\[ \operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2) = \rho\sigma_1\sigma_2 \]

\[ =(0.50)(3)(8) \]

\[ =12. \]

This gives us the covariance needed for the new covariance matrix.

C.4 Generate Data for Each Correlation Setting

We now generate a separate multivariate normal sample for each correlation setting.

We use

\[ n_C=1500 \]

observations for each setting.

n_C <- 1500

C_data <- list()

for (rho in correlation_levels) {

  Sigma_rho <- create_covariance_matrix(rho)

  X_rho <- MASS::mvrnorm(
    n = n_C,
    mu = mu,
    Sigma = Sigma_rho
  )

  C_data[[as.character(rho)]] <- X_rho
}

We now have three simulated datasets:

\[ \rho=0.25, \]

\[ \rho=0.50, \]

and

\[ \rho=0.75. \]

Each dataset has the same mean vector and standard deviations, but a different correlation structure.

C.5 Compare the Correlations Numerically

Before examining the graphs, we calculate the simulated correlation between delivery distance and delivery time for each setting.

C_results <- data.frame(
  Theoretical_Correlation = correlation_levels,
  Simulated_Correlation = sapply(
    correlation_levels,
    function(rho) {
      cor(
        C_data[[as.character(rho)]][, 1],
        C_data[[as.character(rho)]][, 2]
      )
    }
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  C_results,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Theoretical versus simulated correlation"
)
Theoretical versus simulated correlation
Theoretical_Correlation Simulated_Correlation
0.25 0.238
0.50 0.508
0.75 0.747

We expect the simulated correlations to be reasonably close to the values that we specified:

\[ 0.25,\quad0.50,\quad0.75. \]

The simulated values will not normally be exactly equal to the theoretical values.

C.6 Visualize the Effect of Correlation

We now compare delivery distance and delivery time for the three correlation settings.

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

for (rho in correlation_levels) {

  X_rho <- C_data[[as.character(rho)]]

  plot(
    X_rho[, 1],
    X_rho[, 2],
    pch = 16,
    cex = 0.45,
    xlab = "Delivery Distance (km)",
    ylab = "Delivery Time (minutes)",
    main = paste("Correlation =", rho)
  )
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

C.7 Compare the Shape and Orientation

The main purpose of these plots is to compare how the point cloud changes as the correlation increases.

When

\[ \rho=0.25, \]

the relationship is positive but relatively weak. We expect the point cloud to show some upward orientation, but with considerable spread around that direction.

When

\[ \rho=0.50, \]

the positive relationship becomes stronger. We expect a clearer upward orientation in the point cloud.

When

\[ \rho=0.75, \]

the relationship is strong. We expect the observations to become more concentrated around an upward-sloping direction.

The lecture describes this behavior for the bivariate normal distribution: correlation causes probability to concentrate along a line.

Therefore, we expect the progression

\[ \boxed{ 0.25 \rightarrow 0.50 \rightarrow 0.75 } \]

to produce increasingly concentrated upward-oriented point clouds.

C.8 Display the Three Correlation Matrices

We can display the three theoretical correlation matrices used in the simulation.

for (rho in correlation_levels) {

  R_rho <- matrix(
    rho,
    nrow = 3,
    ncol = 3
  )

  diag(R_rho) <- 1

  cat("\nCorrelation =", rho, "\n")
  print(R_rho)
}
## 
## Correlation = 0.25 
##      [,1] [,2] [,3]
## [1,] 1.00 0.25 0.25
## [2,] 0.25 1.00 0.25
## [3,] 0.25 0.25 1.00
## 
## Correlation = 0.5 
##      [,1] [,2] [,3]
## [1,]  1.0  0.5  0.5
## [2,]  0.5  1.0  0.5
## [3,]  0.5  0.5  1.0
## 
## Correlation = 0.75 
##      [,1] [,2] [,3]
## [1,] 1.00 0.75 0.75
## [2,] 0.75 1.00 0.75
## [3,] 0.75 0.75 1.00

The matrices demonstrate exactly what changes between the three experiments.

For \(\rho=0.25\):

\[ R_{0.25}= \begin{bmatrix} 1&0.25&0.25\\ 0.25&1&0.25\\ 0.25&0.25&1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

For \(\rho=0.50\):

\[ R_{0.50}= \begin{bmatrix} 1&0.50&0.50\\ 0.50&1&0.50\\ 0.50&0.50&1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

For \(\rho=0.75\):

\[ R_{0.75}= \begin{bmatrix} 1&0.75&0.75\\ 0.75&1&0.75\\ 0.75&0.75&1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The diagonal remains 1 in all three matrices, while the off-diagonal correlations increase.

C.9 Visualize the Correlation Matrices

We can visualize each theoretical correlation matrix using a correlation plot.

If the corrplot package has not already been installed, it can be installed with:

install.packages("corrplot")

We then load the package:

library(corrplot)

Now we can visualize the three correlation structures.

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

for (rho in correlation_levels) {

  R_rho <- matrix(
    rho,
    nrow = 3,
    ncol = 3
  )

  diag(R_rho) <- 1

  corrplot(
    R_rho,
    method = "color",
    addCoef.col = "black",
    tl.col = "black",
    number.cex = 0.8,
    title = paste("rho =", rho),
    mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0)
  )
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

These plots provide a visual representation of the correlation matrices used in our three simulations.

The diagonal entries remain 1 because every variable is perfectly correlated with itself.

The off-diagonal entries increase from \(0.25\) to \(0.50\) to \(0.75\), representing increasingly strong positive relationships.

C.10 Interpretation

The simulation demonstrates how changing the correlation structure affects the shape and orientation of the simulated multivariate normal observations.

At

\[ \rho=0.25, \]

the relationship between delivery distance and delivery time is positive but relatively weak. The point cloud should therefore have a mild upward orientation.

At

\[ \rho=0.50, \]

the relationship is moderately positive, producing a clearer upward orientation.

At

\[ \rho=0.75, \]

the relationship is strongly positive, causing the observations to become more concentrated around an upward-sloping direction.

The simulated correlations should also be reasonably close to the theoretical values of

\[ 0.25,\quad0.50,\quad0.75. \]

Because the means and standard deviations were kept fixed, the comparison allows us to focus on the effect of changing correlation.

This supports the lecture’s discussion that correlation affects the orientation and concentration of probability in the multivariate normal distribution.

Part D. Linear Combination — 7 points

In the previous parts, we studied the three delivery-operation variables jointly:

\[ X_1=\text{delivery distance (km)}, \]

\[ X_2=\text{delivery time (minutes)}, \]

\[ X_3=\text{fuel consumption (liters)}. \]

We now combine these three variables into a single quantity that represents an operational burden score for our hypothetical logistics company.

The purpose of this part is to apply the linear-combination property of the multivariate normal distribution.

D.1 Constructing the Operational Burden Score

We define the operational burden score as

\[ \boxed{ Y=0.80X_1+2.25X_2+3.50X_3 }. \]

In vector notation, this can be written as

\[ Y=a'X, \]

where

\[ a= \begin{bmatrix} 0.80\\ 2.25\\ 3.50 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The coefficients are hypothetical operational weights. They are not estimated from real company data. Instead, they represent the relative importance of each variable under the scenario we designed.

Distance: \(0.80\)

Distance is still an important part of transportation operations because longer routes require more travel and resources. However, our hypothetical company primarily operates as a middleman between sorting and logistics hubs, transporting relatively large batches.

We assume that the company’s hub locations, available routes, and workforce have already been organized to support efficient movement between hubs. Therefore, distance is important but is not our highest operational priority.

We assign it a weight of

\[ \boxed{0.80}. \]

Timeliness: \(2.25\)

Timely delivery is an important company value because reliable movement between hubs affects the reliability of the overall delivery network.

For a logistics company serving major online-shopping operations, such as large e-commerce platforms, late or failed deliveries can affect service reliability and the company’s reputation with its clients.

Our hypothetical company therefore places a relatively high importance on delivery time. We assume that our routes, hub locations, and available workforce have been optimized partly around maintaining timely operations.

We assign delivery time a weight of

\[ \boxed{2.25}. \]

Fuel consumption: \(3.50\)

Fuel consumption receives the highest weight in our scenario.

We assume that current operating conditions have caused fuel costs to increase, making fuel consumption a particularly significant financial burden for the company.

Because our company operates transportation between hubs, fuel is a direct operating expense. Reducing unnecessary fuel consumption therefore has a substantial effect on the company’s operating burden.

We assign fuel consumption a weight of

\[ \boxed{3.50}. \]

Therefore, our relative operational priorities are

\[ \boxed{ 3.50\text{ (Fuel)} > 2.25\text{ (Timeliness)} > 0.80\text{ (Distance)} }. \]

These weights allow us to represent the current priorities of our hypothetical company within a single score.

D.2 The Linear Combination Property

The multivariate normal distribution has an important property concerning linear combinations.

If

\[ X\sim N_p(\mu,\Sigma), \]

and

\[ Y=a'X, \]

then

\[ \boxed{ Y\sim N(a'\mu,a'\Sigma a) }. \]

Therefore, once we have selected our coefficient vector \(a\), we can calculate the theoretical mean and variance of our operational burden score directly from the \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\) that we defined in Part A.

This allows us to compare the theoretical result with the values obtained from our simulated observations.

D.3 Calculate the Theoretical Mean

From Part A, our mean vector is

\[ \mu= \begin{bmatrix} 12\\ 35\\ 4.5 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Our coefficient vector is

\[ a= \begin{bmatrix} 0.80\\ 2.25\\ 3.50 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The theoretical mean of \(Y\) is

\[ E(Y)=a'\mu. \]

Substituting our values gives

\[ E(Y) = \begin{bmatrix} 0.80&2.25&3.50 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 12\\ 35\\ 4.5 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore,

\[ E(Y) = 0.80(12)+2.25(35)+3.50(4.5). \]

Calculating each contribution,

\[ 0.80(12)=9.6, \]

\[ 2.25(35)=78.75, \]

and

\[ 3.50(4.5)=15.75. \]

Thus,

\[ E(Y)=9.6+78.75+15.75 \]

\[ \boxed{E(Y)=104.10}. \]

We can verify this calculation in R:

a <- c(
  Distance_km = 0.80,
  Delivery_Time_min = 2.25,
  Fuel_Liters = 3.50
)

a
##       Distance_km Delivery_Time_min       Fuel_Liters 
##              0.80              2.25              3.50
theoretical_mean_Y <-
  as.numeric(t(a) %*% mu)

theoretical_mean_Y
## [1] 104.1

The R result should be

\[ \boxed{104.10}. \]

D.4 Calculate the Theoretical Variance

The variance of a linear combination is

\[ \boxed{ \operatorname{Var}(Y)=a'\Sigma a }. \]

This formula is particularly useful here because it incorporates both the individual variances and the covariances among distance, delivery time, and fuel consumption.

From Part A,

\[ \Sigma= \begin{bmatrix} 9&12&2.7\\ 12&64&7.2\\ 2.7&7.2&2.25 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore,

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \begin{bmatrix} 0.80&2.25&3.50 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 9&12&2.7\\ 12&64&7.2\\ 2.7&7.2&2.25 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0.80\\ 2.25\\ 3.50 \end{bmatrix}. \]

We can calculate this directly in R:

theoretical_variance_Y <-
  as.numeric(t(a) %*% Sigma %*% a)

theoretical_variance_Y
## [1] 529.0425

For our chosen coefficients and covariance matrix,

\[ \boxed{ \operatorname{Var}(Y)=a'\Sigma a } \]

and the numerical result produced by R is our theoretical variance.

The corresponding theoretical standard deviation is

theoretical_sd_Y <-
  sqrt(theoretical_variance_Y)

theoretical_sd_Y
## [1] 23.00092

Therefore, our theoretical distribution is

\[ \boxed{ Y\sim N \left( 104.10,\, a'\Sigma a \right) }. \]

The variance value calculated above will be used as the theoretical benchmark for our simulation.

D.5 Why Does the Covariance Matrix Matter?

It is important that we do not interpret

\[ a'\Sigma a \]

as simply adding the three individual variances.

Because our variables are correlated, the covariance terms also contribute to the variance of \(Y\).

For a three-variable linear combination,

\[ Y=a_1X_1+a_2X_2+a_3X_3, \]

the variance can be expanded as

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(Y) ={}&a_1^2\operatorname{Var}(X_1) +a_2^2\operatorname{Var}(X_2) +a_3^2\operatorname{Var}(X_3)\\ &+2a_1a_2\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)\\ &+2a_1a_3\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_3)\\ &+2a_2a_3\operatorname{Cov}(X_2,X_3). \end{aligned} \]

This shows why the covariance structure we defined in Part A matters again in Part D.

The variables do not vary independently. Their relationships contribute to the overall variability of our operational burden score.

D.6 Create the Operational Burden Score from the Simulation

In Part B, we generated the simulated observations and stored them in the data frame X.

We now apply our coefficient vector \(a\) to every simulated observation.

For each delivery,

\[ Y=0.80X_1+2.25X_2+3.50X_3. \]

Y <- as.numeric(
  as.matrix(X) %*% a
)

head(Y)
## [1] 106.7752 133.1502 132.5269 138.6122 136.6273 122.6057

Each value of Y represents the operational burden score for one simulated delivery.

A larger value means that the combination of distance, delivery time, and fuel consumption produces a larger burden according to the weights we defined.

D.7 Compare Theoretical and Simulated Results

We now calculate the sample mean and sample variance of the simulated operational burden scores.

simulated_mean_Y <- mean(Y)

simulated_variance_Y <- var(Y)

simulated_sd_Y <- sd(Y)

linear_combination_comparison <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "Mean",
    "Variance",
    "Standard Deviation"
  ),
  Theoretical = c(
    theoretical_mean_Y,
    theoretical_variance_Y,
    theoretical_sd_Y
  ),
  Simulated = c(
    simulated_mean_Y,
    simulated_variance_Y,
    simulated_sd_Y
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  linear_combination_comparison,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Theoretical versus simulated operational burden score"
)
Theoretical versus simulated operational burden score
Quantity Theoretical Simulated
Mean 104.100 104.219
Variance 529.042 528.220
Standard Deviation 23.001 22.983

We expect the simulated mean to be reasonably close to

\[ 104.10 \]

and the simulated variance to be reasonably close to the theoretical value calculated from

\[ a'\Sigma a. \]

D.8 Visualize the Operational Burden Score

We now examine the simulated distribution of \(Y\).

hist(
  Y,
  breaks = 40,
  probability = TRUE,
  main = "Operational Burden Score",
  xlab = expression(
    Y == 0.80*X[1] + 2.25*X[2] + 3.50*X[3]
  )
)

curve(
  dnorm(
    x,
    mean = theoretical_mean_Y,
    sd = theoretical_sd_Y
  ),
  add = TRUE,
  lwd = 2
)

abline(
  v = theoretical_mean_Y,
  lty = 2,
  lwd = 2
)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c(
    "Theoretical normal density",
    "Theoretical mean"
  ),
  lty = c(1, 2),
  lwd = 2,
  bty = "n"
)

The histogram shows the simulated values of the operational burden score.

The overlaid normal density represents the theoretical distribution

\[ Y\sim N(a'\mu,a'\Sigma a). \]

The vertical line represents the theoretical mean

\[ E(Y)=104.10. \]

The purpose of the visualization is to compare the empirical simulated distribution with the theoretical normal distribution predicted by the linear-combination property.

D.9 Interpretation

Our operational burden score is

\[ Y=0.80X_1+2.25X_2+3.50X_3. \]

The coefficients represent the relative priorities of our hypothetical logistics company.

Distance has the lowest weight of \(0.80\), because although distance still affects transportation operations, the company’s hub-based network has been organized to reduce the importance of distance relative to other operational concerns.

Timeliness has a weight of \(2.25\), reflecting the importance of reliable and timely movement between hubs for maintaining service reliability and reputation.

Fuel has the largest weight of \(3.50\), representing the increased financial burden caused by higher fuel costs in our hypothetical current operating environment.

The theoretical linear-combination result states that

\[ Y\sim N(a'\mu,a'\Sigma a). \]

We therefore compare the theoretical mean and variance calculated using \(a'\mu\) and \(a'\Sigma a\) with the corresponding sample statistics from the simulated observations.

Part E. Mahalanobis Distance — 7 points

In Parts A and B, we defined and simulated our three-variable multivariate normal distribution:

\[ X\sim N_3(\mu,\Sigma). \]

We now investigate how far an observation is from the center of this multivariate distribution.

The purpose of this part is to use Mahalanobis distance, which accounts for both the variability of the variables and their covariance structure.

E.1 Why Do We Need Mahalanobis Distance?

Suppose we have one simulated delivery represented by

\[ x= \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

A simple way to measure its distance from the mean would be to use ordinary Euclidean distance.

However, our three variables have different variances and are correlated.

For example, delivery time has a theoretical variance of

\[ 64, \]

while fuel consumption has a theoretical variance of only

\[ 2.25. \]

Therefore, a difference of the same numerical size does not necessarily represent the same level of unusualness for the two variables.

Mahalanobis distance takes the covariance structure into account.

For an observation \(x\), the squared Mahalanobis distance is

\[ \boxed{ D^2=(x-\mu)'\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu) }. \]

The inverse covariance matrix \(\Sigma^{-1}\) adjusts the distance based on the variability and relationships among the variables.

E.2 Our Mean Vector and Covariance Matrix

We use the same theoretical population established in Part A:

\[ \mu= \begin{bmatrix} 12\\ 35\\ 4.5 \end{bmatrix} \]

and

\[ \Sigma= \begin{bmatrix} 9&12&2.7\\ 12&64&7.2\\ 2.7&7.2&2.25 \end{bmatrix}. \]

We do not create a new distribution for Part E.

Instead, we use the same simulated observations generated in Part B.

This allows the Mahalanobis-distance analysis to remain connected to the same multivariate normal population used throughout the previous parts.

E.3 Calculate the Inverse Covariance Matrix

The Mahalanobis-distance formula uses

\[ \Sigma^{-1}. \]

We calculate the inverse of our covariance matrix using solve().

Sigma_inverse <- solve(Sigma)

round(Sigma_inverse, 4)
##                   Distance_km Delivery_Time_min Fuel_Liters
## Distance_km            0.1823           -0.0150     -0.1709
## Delivery_Time_min     -0.0150            0.0256     -0.0641
## Fuel_Liters           -0.1709           -0.0641      0.8547

The resulting matrix is the inverse covariance matrix used to adjust the distance calculation.

E.4 Calculate the Squared Mahalanobis Distance

For each simulated observation, we calculate

\[ D^2=(x-\mu)'\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu). \]

First, we center every observation by subtracting the theoretical mean vector:

\[ X-\mu. \]

X_centered <- sweep(
  as.matrix(X),
  2,
  mu,
  "-"
)

We then calculate the squared Mahalanobis distance for every simulated observation.

D2 <- rowSums(
  (X_centered %*% Sigma_inverse) *
    X_centered
)

head(D2)
## [1] 4.7921637 3.0493561 6.2115978 3.7193136 4.0728038 0.9552007

Each value in D2 represents the squared Mahalanobis distance of one simulated delivery from the theoretical center of the population.

A smaller value indicates that an observation is relatively close to the center after accounting for the covariance structure.

A larger value indicates that the observation is farther from the center in covariance-adjusted terms.

E.5 Theoretical Distribution of \(D^2\)

The theoretical result for a multivariate normal distribution is

\[ X\sim N_p(\mu,\Sigma) \]

implies

\[ \boxed{ D^2\sim\chi_p^2 }. \]

Our distribution contains three variables:

\[ p=3. \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{ D^2\sim\chi_3^2 }. \]

This gives us a theoretical distribution against which we can compare the simulated Mahalanobis distances.

E.6 Compare the Mean of \(D^2\)

A chi-square distribution with \(p\) degrees of freedom has theoretical mean

\[ E(D^2)=p. \]

Since our distribution has

\[ p=3, \]

we expect

\[ \boxed{E(D^2)=3}. \]

We calculate the simulated mean:

theoretical_mean_D2 <- 3

simulated_mean_D2 <- mean(D2)

mahalanobis_mean_comparison <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "Theoretical mean of D^2",
    "Simulated mean of D^2"
  ),
  Value = c(
    theoretical_mean_D2,
    simulated_mean_D2
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  mahalanobis_mean_comparison,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Theoretical versus simulated mean of squared Mahalanobis distance"
)
Theoretical versus simulated mean of squared Mahalanobis distance
Quantity Value
Theoretical mean of D^2 3.00
Simulated mean of D^2 2.99

We expect the simulated mean to be reasonably close to

\[ 3. \]

It does not need to be exactly 3 because the simulated data form a finite random sample.

E.7 Construct the 90% Probability Region

We now construct a 90% probability region.

Since

\[ D^2\sim\chi_3^2, \]

the 90% cutoff is the 90th percentile of the chi-square distribution with 3 degrees of freedom:

\[ \boxed{ c=\chi_3^2(0.90) }. \]

We calculate this cutoff in R using qchisq().

chi_square_cutoff_90 <- qchisq(
  0.90,
  df = 3
)

chi_square_cutoff_90
## [1] 6.251389

Therefore, the 90% probability region is

\[ \boxed{ (x-\mu)'\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu) \leq \chi_3^2(0.90) }. \]

In words, observations whose squared Mahalanobis distance is below this cutoff belong to the theoretical 90% probability region.

E.8 Check the Simulated Proportion Inside the Region

We now determine how many of our simulated observations fall within the 90% region.

inside_90 <- D2 <= chi_square_cutoff_90

simulated_proportion_90 <- mean(inside_90)

region_comparison <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "Theoretical proportion",
    "Simulated proportion"
  ),
  Proportion = c(
    0.90,
    simulated_proportion_90
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  region_comparison,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Theoretical versus simulated 90% probability region"
)
Theoretical versus simulated 90% probability region
Quantity Proportion
Theoretical proportion 0.9000
Simulated proportion 0.9066

The theoretical proportion is

\[ 0.90. \]

We therefore expect approximately 90% of the simulated observations to satisfy

\[ D^2\leq\chi_3^2(0.90). \]

The simulated proportion may differ slightly from 0.90 because our simulation contains a finite number of observations.

E.9 Identify Observations Outside the 90% Region

Observations with

\[ D^2>\chi_3^2(0.90) \]

are outside the theoretical 90% probability region.

We can count these observations:

number_outside_90 <- sum(!inside_90)

percentage_outside_90 <- mean(!inside_90) * 100

outside_summary <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "Number outside 90% region",
    "Percentage outside 90% region"
  ),
  Value = c(
    number_outside_90,
    percentage_outside_90
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  outside_summary,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Simulated observations outside the 90% probability region"
)
Simulated observations outside the 90% probability region
Quantity Value
Number outside 90% region 467.00
Percentage outside 90% region 9.34

The theoretical percentage outside the 90% region is

\[ 10\%. \]

Therefore, we expect approximately 10% of the simulated observations to fall outside the region.

These observations are not automatically errors or invalid deliveries. They simply have relatively large covariance-adjusted distances from the center of the population.

E.10 Visualize the Distribution of \(D^2\)

We now compare the simulated distribution of squared Mahalanobis distances with the theoretical \(\chi_3^2\) distribution.

hist(
  D2,
  breaks = 40,
  probability = TRUE,
  main = expression(
    "Squared Mahalanobis Distance and " * chi[3]^2
  ),
  xlab = expression(D^2)
)

curve(
  dchisq(x, df = 3),
  add = TRUE,
  lwd = 2
)

abline(
  v = chi_square_cutoff_90,
  lty = 2,
  lwd = 2
)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c(
    expression(chi[3]^2 ~ " theoretical density"),
    "90% cutoff"
  ),
  lty = c(1, 2),
  lwd = 2,
  bty = "n"
)

The histogram represents the simulated values of

\[ D^2. \]

The overlaid curve represents the theoretical

\[ \chi_3^2 \]

density.

The vertical line represents the 90% chi-square cutoff.

We are therefore visually comparing the empirical distribution from our simulation with the theoretical distribution predicted by the multivariate normal model.

E.11 Why Does the Chi-Square Distribution Appear?

The Mahalanobis-distance result can be understood by standardizing the multivariate normal vector.

The squared Mahalanobis distance

\[ D^2=(X-\mu)'\Sigma^{-1}(X-\mu) \]

accounts for the covariance structure of \(X\).

For a \(p\)-dimensional multivariate normal distribution, this quantity has a chi-square distribution with \(p\) degrees of freedom:

\[ D^2\sim\chi_p^2. \]

Since our model contains three variables,

\[ p=3, \]

so

\[ \boxed{D^2\sim\chi_3^2}. \]

This is why the chi-square distribution is the theoretical reference for our simulation.

E.12 Interpretation

The Mahalanobis-distance analysis measures how unusual each simulated delivery is relative to the center of the multivariate distribution.

Unlike ordinary distance, the Mahalanobis distance accounts for the different variances of distance, delivery time, and fuel consumption, as well as their covariance structure.

For our three-variable model,

\[ D^2\sim\chi_3^2. \]

Therefore, the theoretical mean of \(D^2\) is

\[ 3. \]

We compare this theoretical value with the simulated mean.

We also use the 90th percentile of the \(\chi_3^2\) distribution to construct a theoretical 90% probability region. Approximately 90% of observations from the theoretical population should fall within this region, while approximately 10% should fall outside it.

The simulated results should be reasonably close to these theoretical values. Differences are expected because the simulation contains a finite number of randomly generated observations.

The histogram provides an additional visual comparison between the simulated squared Mahalanobis distances and the theoretical \(\chi_3^2\) distribution.

Part F. Custom Investigation — Conditional Distribution — 5 points

For our custom investigation, we use Option C: Conditional Distribution.

We investigate the distribution of one variable when another variable is fixed at a particular value.

For our delivery-operation scenario, we investigate the relationship between:

\[ X_1=\text{fuel consumption (liters)} \]

and

\[ X_2=\text{delivery time (minutes)}. \]

We investigate

\[ \boxed{X_1\mid X_2=60}. \]

In other words, we ask:

When a delivery takes 1 hour (60 minutes), what fuel consumption should we expect?

This is useful for our logistics scenario because longer delivery times may be associated with greater fuel consumption. The conditional distribution allows us to determine the expected fuel consumption and remaining variability when the delivery time is known.

F.1 Why Condition on Delivery Time?

From Part A, our theoretical mean vector is

\[ \mu= \begin{bmatrix} 12\\ 35\\ 4.5 \end{bmatrix}. \]

For this investigation, we focus on

\[ X_1=\text{Fuel Consumption} \]

and

\[ X_2=\text{Delivery Time}. \]

The relevant theoretical means are therefore

\[ \mu_1=4.5 \]

and

\[ \mu_2=35. \]

From the covariance matrix defined in Part A,

\[ \Sigma= \begin{bmatrix} 9&12&2.7\\ 12&64&7.2\\ 2.7&7.2&2.25 \end{bmatrix}, \]

the relevant covariance values are

\[ \sigma_{11}=2.25, \]

\[ \sigma_{22}=64, \]

and

\[ \sigma_{12}=7.2. \]

The covariance between fuel consumption and delivery time is positive:

\[ \sigma_{12}=7.2>0. \]

Therefore, our theoretical model indicates a positive relationship between delivery time and fuel consumption.

For our investigation, we choose

\[ \boxed{x_2=60\text{ minutes}}. \]

This represents a one-hour delivery, which is substantially longer than our theoretical average delivery time of

\[ 35\text{ minutes}. \]

We can therefore investigate how a relatively long delivery time affects the expected fuel consumption.

F.2 Theoretical Conditional Mean

The conditional expectation formula given in the FA3 instructions is

\[ E(X_1\mid X_2=x_2) = \mu_1+ \frac{\sigma_{12}}{\sigma_{22}} (x_2-\mu_2). \]

For our variables and \(x_2=60\),

\[ E(X_1\mid X_2=60) = 4.5+ \frac{7.2}{64}(60-35). \]

Since

\[ 60-35=25, \]

we obtain

\[ E(X_1\mid X_2=60) = 4.5+ \frac{7.2}{64}(25). \]

Therefore,

\[ E(X_1\mid X_2=60) = 4.5+2.8125 \]

and

\[ \boxed{ E(X_1\mid X_2=60)=7.3125 }. \]

Thus, according to our theoretical model, a delivery taking one hour has an expected fuel consumption of approximately

\[ \boxed{7.31\text{ liters}}. \]

We calculate this in R:

x2_fixed <- 60

conditional_mean <-
  mu["Fuel_Liters"] +
  Sigma["Fuel_Liters", "Delivery_Time_min"] /
  Sigma["Delivery_Time_min", "Delivery_Time_min"] *
  (x2_fixed - mu["Delivery_Time_min"])

conditional_mean
## Fuel_Liters 
##      7.3125

F.3 Theoretical Conditional Variance

The conditional variance formula given

\[ \operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid X_2) = \sigma_{11} - \frac{\sigma_{12}^2}{\sigma_{22}}. \]

Substituting our values gives

\[ \operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid X_2) = 2.25-\frac{7.2^2}{64}. \]

Since

\[ 7.2^2=51.84, \]

we obtain

\[ \operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid X_2) = 2.25-\frac{51.84}{64}. \]

Therefore,

\[ \operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid X_2) = 2.25-0.81 \]

\[ \boxed{ \operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid X_2)=1.44 }. \]

The corresponding conditional standard deviation is

\[ \sqrt{1.44}=1.2. \]

Therefore, our theoretical conditional distribution is

\[ \boxed{ X_1\mid X_2=60 \sim N(7.3125,1.44) }. \]

We calculate the conditional variance and standard deviation in R:

conditional_variance <-
  Sigma["Fuel_Liters", "Fuel_Liters"] -
  Sigma["Fuel_Liters", "Delivery_Time_min"]^2 /
  Sigma["Delivery_Time_min", "Delivery_Time_min"]

conditional_sd <- sqrt(conditional_variance)

conditional_variance
## [1] 1.44
conditional_sd
## [1] 1.2

F.4 Interpreting the Conditional Mean

Our overall theoretical mean for fuel consumption is

\[ E(X_1)=4.5\text{ L}. \]

When we condition on a delivery time of 60 minutes, the theoretical expected fuel consumption becomes

\[ E(X_1\mid X_2=60)=7.3125\text{ L}. \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{ 7.3125>4.5 }. \]

This increase occurs because our model specifies a positive covariance between delivery time and fuel consumption:

\[ \sigma_{12}=7.2>0. \]

The one-hour condition is also above the theoretical average delivery time:

\[ 60>35. \]

Therefore, the conditional mean shifts upward from the overall fuel mean.

This allows us to demonstrate how information about one variable can change the expected value of another variable when the variables are related.

F.5 Select Simulated Observations Near 60 Minutes

The simulated delivery times are continuous values, so it is unlikely that many observations will have exactly

\[ X_2=60. \]

Instead, we approximate the conditional distribution by selecting observations within a small interval around 60 minutes:

\[ 59.5\leq X_2\leq60.5. \]

window <- 0.5

conditional_sample <- X[
  abs(
    X$Delivery_Time_min - x2_fixed
  ) <= window,
]

nrow(conditional_sample)
## [1] 1

The selected observations represent simulated deliveries with times approximately equal to one hour.

We can inspect the selected fuel-consumption values:

head(
  conditional_sample$Fuel_Liters
)
## [1] 7.918756

F.6 Calculate the Simulated Conditional Statistics

We now calculate the sample mean, variance, and standard deviation of fuel consumption among the selected observations.

simulated_conditional_mean <-
  mean(conditional_sample$Fuel_Liters)

simulated_conditional_variance <-
  var(conditional_sample$Fuel_Liters)

simulated_conditional_sd <-
  sd(conditional_sample$Fuel_Liters)

conditional_comparison <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "Conditional Mean",
    "Conditional Variance",
    "Conditional Standard Deviation"
  ),
  Theoretical = c(
    conditional_mean,
    conditional_variance,
    conditional_sd
  ),
  Simulated = c(
    simulated_conditional_mean,
    simulated_conditional_variance,
    simulated_conditional_sd
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  conditional_comparison,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Theoretical versus simulated conditional distribution"
)
Theoretical versus simulated conditional distribution
Quantity Theoretical Simulated
Conditional Mean 7.312 7.919
Conditional Variance 1.440 NA
Conditional Standard Deviation 1.200 NA

We expect the simulated conditional mean and variance to be reasonably close to the theoretical values

\[ 5.625 \]

and

\[ 1.44. \]

The actual theoretical mean for our 60-minute condition is instead

\[ \boxed{7.3125}. \]

The simulated values will not necessarily be exactly equal to the theoretical values because the simulated conditional sample is finite and uses a small interval around 60 minutes rather than the exact mathematical condition \(X_2=60\).

F.7 Visualize the Conditional Distribution

We now visualize the simulated fuel consumption for deliveries whose delivery times are approximately 60 minutes.

hist(
  conditional_sample$Fuel_Liters,
  breaks = 25,
  probability = TRUE,
  main = "Fuel Consumption Given Delivery Time Near 60 Minutes",
  xlab = "Fuel Consumption (liters)"
)

curve(
  dnorm(
    x,
    mean = conditional_mean,
    sd = conditional_sd
  ),
  add = TRUE,
  lwd = 2
)

abline(
  v = conditional_mean,
  lty = 2,
  lwd = 2
)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c(
    "Theoretical conditional normal density",
    "Theoretical conditional mean"
  ),
  lty = c(1, 2),
  lwd = 2,
  bty = "n"
)

The histogram represents the simulated fuel consumption for deliveries with times close to one hour.

The overlaid curve represents the theoretical conditional normal distribution

\[ N(7.3125,1.44). \]

The vertical line represents the theoretical conditional mean

\[ 7.3125. \]

The visualization allows us to compare the empirical conditional distribution obtained from the simulation with the theoretical conditional distribution.

F.8 Compare Unconditional and Conditional Fuel Consumption

It is useful to compare the overall fuel-consumption mean with the conditional mean.

The unconditional theoretical mean is

\[ E(X_1)=4.5. \]

When we condition on

\[ X_2=60, \]

the expected fuel consumption becomes

\[ E(X_1\mid X_2=60)=7.3125. \]

The increase is therefore

\[ 7.3125-4.5=2.8125\text{ L}. \]

We can calculate this in R:

mean_increase <-
  conditional_mean - mu["Fuel_Liters"]

percentage_increase <-
  (mean_increase / mu["Fuel_Liters"]) * 100

comparison <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "Unconditional fuel mean",
    "Conditional fuel mean",
    "Increase",
    "Percentage increase"
  ),
  Value = c(
    mu["Fuel_Liters"],
    conditional_mean,
    mean_increase,
    percentage_increase
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  comparison,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Change in expected fuel consumption after conditioning on a 60-minute delivery"
)
Change in expected fuel consumption after conditioning on a 60-minute delivery
Quantity Value
Unconditional fuel mean 4.500
Conditional fuel mean 7.312
Increase 2.812
Percentage increase 62.500

Thus, our model predicts a higher expected fuel consumption when the delivery time is fixed at one hour.

F.9 Interpretation

Our custom investigation examined the conditional distribution

\[ X_1\mid X_2=60, \]

where \(X_1\) represents fuel consumption and \(X_2\) represents delivery time.

The theoretical conditional mean is

\[ \boxed{ E(X_1\mid X_2=60)=7.3125 } \]

liters.

The theoretical conditional variance is

\[ \boxed{ \operatorname{Var}(X_1\mid X_2)=1.44 }. \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{ X_1\mid X_2=60 \sim N(7.3125,1.44) }. \]

The conditional mean is higher than the overall theoretical fuel consumption mean of

\[ 4.5\text{ L}. \]

This occurs because a delivery time of 60 minutes is above the theoretical average of 35 minutes, and our model specifies a positive relationship between delivery time and fuel consumption.

In our hypothetical logistics scenario, this means that deliveries taking approximately one hour are expected to require more fuel than a typical delivery.

We compare the theoretical conditional distribution with simulated observations whose delivery times are close to 60 minutes.

The simulated conditional statistics should be reasonably close to the theoretical values. Differences are expected because the simulation is finite and because we approximate the exact condition \(X_2=60\) using a small interval around 60 minutes.
